summary: A guide for newcomers to the IETF. It describes how IETF meetings and working groups work, related organizations, and the standards process. It was replaced by RFC 4677.

plainLanguage.summary: It's a beginner's handbook for joining a big club that writes Internet rules.

subtitle: A practical guide to understanding IETF meetings, working groups, and the Internet standards process.

tldr.problem: The IETF is growing rapidly with many newcomers each meeting. The inner workings of IETF meetings, working groups, and the standards process are not well-documented or obvious to newcomers.
tldr.mechanism: This guide describes the IETF hierarchy (ISOC, IESG, IAB, IANA, RFC Editor), explains how meetings and working groups function, and walks through the standards track process from Internet Drafts to RFCs.
tldr.outcome: Newcomers gain practical knowledge to participate effectively in IETF activities, contributing to better standards development.

today: RFC 3160 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 4677. This FYI document remains valuable as a historical overview of IETF structure and process, though readers should consult current IETF documentation and BCPs for the latest procedures and organization details.

sections.title: What Is the IETF?
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is a loosely self-organized group of volunteers who contribute to the engineering and evolution of Internet technologies. It is the principal body engaged in developing new Internet standard specifications. Uniquely, the IETF exists as a collection of happenings but is not a corporation—it has no board of directors, no members, and no dues.

The IETF's mission includes identifying and proposing solutions to pressing operational and technical problems in the Internet, specifying protocols and near-term architecture, making recommendations to the IESG about standardization, facilitating technology transfer from research to the community, and providing a forum for information exchange among vendors, users, researchers, and network managers.

Volunteers meet three times per year at face-to-face meetings. Participation is open to anyone; there is no membership in the IETF, though being on IETF or Working Group mailing lists is the closest equivalent.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF is a group of engineers who volunteer to write and improve Internet standards. Anyone can join by signing up for mailing lists or attending meetings. It has no president or permanent office, just people who meet to solve problems.

sections.title: The IETF Hierarchy
sections.content:
The IETF operates within a structured hierarchy of supporting organizations. The Internet Society (ISOC) is a non-profit membership organization that provides financial and legal support. IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) manages technical IETF activities and the standards process through Area Directors selected by a Nominations Committee. Areas include Applications, General, Internet, Operations & Management, Routing, Security, Transport, and User Services.

The IAB (Internet Architecture Board) oversees the big picture, reviews new working group charters for architectural consistency, and sponsors the Internet Research Task Force. The IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) maintains protocol registries (TCP ports, MIME types, etc.). The RFC Editor formats and publishes RFCs, maintaining the definitive repository. The IETF Secretariat provides logistical support for meetings and mailing lists.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF has different groups that do different jobs: one runs the meetings, one decides what becomes a standard, one watches the big picture, one keeps track of numbers like port numbers, one publishes the official documents.

sections.title: IETF Meetings
sections.content:
IETF meetings are held three times per year in different cities, with participants from vendors, users, researchers, and network operators. Meetings are not conferences but rather working sessions focused on advancing standards work.

Registration is required. Newcomers are welcomed with orientation sessions explaining the meeting structure and IETF culture. Sessions include working group meetings (where most work happens), research presentations, and social events. The meeting agenda lists working groups and their meeting times. Proceedings are published afterward.

For newcomers, the document describes what different participants (IS Managers, Network Operators, Vendors, Academics, Press) might find relevant. A newcomers' orientation helps first-time attendees understand the flow and culture. The document covers practical details: dress code (casual), avoiding "spots before your eyes" (the information booth), the Terminal Room, meals, and social events.
sections.plainLanguage: IETF meetings happen three times a year. People show up, attend working group sessions where they discuss standards, eat meals together, and attend social events. There's no formal presentation stage; it's mostly people meeting and working.

sections.title: Working Groups and the Standards Process
sections.content:
Working Groups (WGs) are the core units where IETF work happens. Each WG has a charter defining its scope and is led by one or more chairs. WGs use mailing lists for most work, with face-to-face meetings at IETF meetings and sometimes interim meetings between plenary sessions.

Working group chairs manage discussions, ensure rough consensus is reached, and shepherd documents through the standards process. Participants prepare documents for discussion before meetings, reducing meeting time spent on basics and increasing productivity.

Birds of a Feather (BOFs) sessions explore potential new work areas. If consensus forms, a BOF can transition to a formal working group.

The standards process moves Internet Drafts through IESG review. Documents must achieve rough consensus in the working group. Standards-Track RFCs require specific sections (MUST/SHOULD/MAY keywords, normative references, IANA Considerations, Security Considerations). Informational and Experimental RFCs follow simpler paths.
sections.plainLanguage: Working groups are teams that focus on one topic. They talk on mailing lists and meet in person at IETF meetings. A chair runs each group and helps move their document toward becoming an official standard.

sections.title: RFCs and the Internet Standards Track
sections.content:
An Internet Draft is a working document that can be submitted for standardization. Internet Drafts are temporary; they are discarded after six months unless updated.

Standards-Track RFCs progress from Proposed Standard, through Draft Standard, to Internet Standard. Each stage requires IETF consensus and IESG approval. Standards-Track documents require RFC 2119 keywords (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) to clearly state requirements. They must include normative references (specs you must implement), IANA Considerations (registry items), and Security Considerations sections.

Informational RFCs provide information but don't specify standards. Experimental RFCs describe protocols under investigation. FYI documents provide topical overviews for broad audiences. BCPs (Best Current Practices) make recommendations for how the Internet should be operated.

The author handles early versions; the RFC Editor takes over once an RFC is approved, formatting and publishing it. Once published, an RFC is never revised—updates come in new RFCs that "obsolete" or "update" the original.
sections.plainLanguage: Documents start as drafts, get discussed and improved, then go through review. If they're standards, they need sections about security and special features. Once published as an RFC, they never change—new versions get new numbers.
